title: Loops

writing.exampleCaption: `break` returns `count` as the value of the `loop` expression.
writing.explanation:
`for` consumes an iterator, `while` repeats while a condition remains true, and `loop` has no condition at all. A `loop` expression can return a value with `break value`. `continue` skips directly to the next iteration. Selecting the narrowest form makes termination easier to see and accidental infinite work harder to write.

The example chooses `loop` because the end condition is written inside the body. `count` starts at zero, increases once per pass, and when it reaches three, `break count` exits with the value `3`. That value becomes `answer`. A bare `break` would yield `()`, so the type of `answer` depends on what every possible exit produces. This is a `loop` expression, not just a repeated statement.

For a known sequence, `for` usually says more with less code: it asks an iterator for the next item and stops when there are none. `while` repeats while its boolean condition remains true; it is useful when the condition itself is the central idea. An unconditional `loop` makes sense when the body must inspect data before deciding to stop, but every path through it should have a comprehensible exit plan. `continue` jumps to the next pass without running the remainder of the current body.

Trace `count` on paper for each iteration and mark exactly where the `break` happens. Then rewrite a three-pass task with `for index in 0..3` and compare the two versions. If you remove the `break` from the original loop, ask whether the program can ever finish. The most readable loop is the one whose termination rule a reader can see immediately.

When choosing a loop form, ask whether the collection owns the elements after iteration. Iterating over `&items` borrows; iterating over `items` can move its elements. Try both and inspect whether the original collection is still available after the loop.

Choose a loop based on what controls repetition. A `for` loop is natural when you already have a range or collection to traverse. A `while` loop repeats while a condition stays true. A plain `loop` continues until a `break` or other exit. Whichever form you choose, identify the state that changes and the condition that eventually stops the work. An accidental infinite loop is usually a missing state update or a boundary that can never be reached.

Trace the example for all three iterations in a table: `count` before, condition, body effect, `count` after. Then run your `for` rewrite over an empty range and a one-item range and count the passes. If you need both position and value, `enumerate()` often reads better than manual indexing. A `break` can also return a value from `loop`; a `continue` skips to the next iteration. Use each only when it makes the exit path easier to see.
writing.feedback: A value after break becomes the value produced by the `loop` expression.

recall.question: What does this print?
recall.answer: `9`. `continue` skips the rest of the body for even numbers, so only `1 + 3 + 5` is added.

recall.question: Why does the last line fail to compile, and what is the fix?
recall.answer: `for name in names` consumes the vector and moves its elements, so `names` is gone afterwards: E0382 borrow of moved value. Iterate over `&names` to borrow the elements instead.
